name: Ben Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the independent Work Futures Panel, which has no ties to employers or AI firms. What you say is confidential; could you walk me through a normal day on site?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Ben, 27, a site carpenter and working team lead on a mid-rise project near the old rail yard. I check the drawings with our foreman, split the work, then I'm measuring, cutting and fixing alongside the crew.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of the work suits you, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like when a crooked opening finally takes a square frame because you've read the timber right. The tiring bit is carrying gear up unfinished stairs and waiting when another trade blocks the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The interviewer reads the card for AI Plateau: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew the phone tools might save a few minutes on drawings, but the saw still needs a steady hand. People will repeat the big AI stories, though our site looks much like last Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My wage and hours look steady in this picture, and I've got several months put away. I'm not keen to learn another app just because the office likes it; I trust a marked-up plan I can hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep leading the carpentry crew and check any new drawing feature with the foreman before relying on it. I'll leave my savings where they are and keep my usual work routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels calm for my own job, with a little irritation at another screen asking for attention. I still like seeing the frame fit without a machine deciding where it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which person on your crew would you talk with first, and what would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Luis, our foreman, whether the new drawing tool changes the latest revision or only formats it. He's the one who catches a changed measurement before we cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner over dinner that you would leave out of a site conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner I don't think our pay is under threat from a small time-saving tool. I'd also admit I don't want to spend evenings learning software that barely affects my work.

say: **I expect** small software gains to change schedules before they change the work in my hands.
**I won't claim** a small tool threatens my wage or hours.
think: **My pay** looks steady in this picture, and my reserve gives me room.
**I still prefer** a marked-up drawing to another screen.
do: Keep **leading the carpentry crew** and check new drawing features with the foreman.
Leave my **reserve untouched** while I follow the usual site routine.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own income, with a little irritation at another screen.
S0.quote: My wage and hours look steady in this picture, and I've got several months put away.
fieldNote: Ben links the **minor change** to schedules rather than his current carpentry hours.
His **substantial reserve** makes his calm about income credible in this scenario.
He shows **resistance** to new software and prefers a drawing he can mark by hand.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew on current projects
Wait for the foreman to confirm real tools are in use

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The interviewer reads the card for Steady Disruption: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office may use AI to write schedules and check orders, but the site still needs people who can set out a wall. I wouldn't claim nothing will change, because fewer delays could mean fewer hands on some jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My hands-on hours seem safer than the planning tasks, but my team-lead paperwork could shrink. I have savings and plenty of nearby projects, yet I don't want a computer deciding the crew size without a person checking the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the foreman to show me any AI schedule before it affects our sequence, and I'll learn only the parts that help me read the current drawings. I'll keep my lead role and look at local openings if my paid hours fall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about the paperwork changing and calm about fitting timber today. I don't like being made to depend on a system I haven't seen work on a wet, crowded floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which person on your crew would you talk with first, and what would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my colleague Niko which of his jobs has already moved from phone calls to software. If buying and booking are automated, I want to know whether delivery mistakes get fixed faster or land on us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner over dinner that you would leave out of a site conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that I can likely find another site nearby, but changing employers could mean losing the crew I know. I would not say that a team lead title guarantees work.

say: **I can say** site carpentry still needs a person who can set out a wall.
**I won't promise** that fewer delays leave every crew size unchanged.
think: **My lead paperwork** could shrink even if the hands-on work remains.
**I have nearby options**, but I dislike software setting crew numbers without a site check.
do: Ask the foreman to show me any **AI schedule** before it changes our sequence.
Check **nearby carpentry openings** if my paid hours fall.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about paperwork changing, though fitting timber still feels familiar.
S1.quote: I wouldn't claim nothing will change, because fewer delays could mean fewer hands on some jobs.
fieldNote: He distinguishes hands-on work from **team-lead paperwork**, which may change sooner.
**Nearby openings** and savings give him some control if hours fall.
His **reluctance** to trust unseen tools remains clear.

steps.text: Keep leading the carpentry crew while paid site work remains
Learn the AI scheduling features needed to read current drawings
Check nearby carpentry openings if paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The interviewer reads the card for AGI by 2028: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people that if thinking work is that capable by 2028, the office side of building will change before robots reach our tools. We have until about 2031 before the card puts hands-on work at the same level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My carpentry skill gives me time, not a permanent shield; by 2031 a robot could handle the physical work too. I have a cushion and local options, but I expect some jobs to disappear and would need to compete for the rest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep working on site through 2028 and ask the foreman which projects are funded for the next year. I'll compare nearby carpentry jobs and keep my reserve intact while I watch for actual robot trials.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious about losing hours once robots arrive, though I can act while there are still projects around. The short warning makes it hard to picture a second trade before 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which person on your crew would you talk with first, and what would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Luis whether our contractor has ordered a robot or only received a sales pitch. That answer changes whether I prepare for a real site change or ignore another demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner over dinner that you would leave out of a site conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner I might have to leave carpentry by 2031, even if we don't know which jobs remain. I'd be embarrassed to admit my team-lead experience might not carry over.

say: **I would tell** the crew that thinking work changes by 2028, before robots reach our tools.
**I would ask** contractors to explain what happens to paid site hours.
think: **My carpentry** buys time, but robots may compete for the physical work around 2031.
**My savings** help, though some jobs may disappear before then.
do: Keep **working on site** through 2028 and ask which following projects are funded.
Compare **nearby carpentry jobs** while preserving existing savings and watching for real robot trials.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing hours after robots arrive, but I can act before then.
S2.quote: My carpentry skill gives me time, not a permanent shield; by 2031 a robot could handle the physical work too.
fieldNote: He identifies **2028** as the date for thinking tasks and 2031 for hands-on robots.
He expects **competition** for jobs but names a practical first check with the foreman.
His **savings** help him plan without making the threat disappear.

steps.text: Keep working on funded carpentry projects through 2028
Compare nearby carpentry jobs while current wages continue
Keep existing reserves intact while watching for real robot trials

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The interviewer reads the card for AGI by 2031: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives a crew time to watch the first systems and plan a careful handover. The thinking AI arrives in 2031, while the hands-on robots are around 2034, so site work gets a short extra window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job could still go after 2034, and I shouldn't pretend planning a site will stay human work after 2031. The extra years help me build savings, but don't tell me what a reliable next job is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my current role for now, ask the foreman yearly what equipment is actually being used, and set aside part of each pay for a transition. In 2032 I'll review local work again rather than assume a course will protect me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but less cornered than in the 2028 picture. I can use the warning years to make decisions with evidence instead of jumping at a rumor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which person on your crew would you talk with first, and what would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Niko whether he would stay on a site where robots do the fitting, or move before that date. I want his honest answer, not a brave one in front of the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner over dinner that you would leave out of a site conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that 2031 is close enough to take seriously but far enough to save. I wouldn't promise that we can just buy a house or switch careers safely.

say: **I would say** five years gives crews time to see changes before robots arrive.
**I would not call** any trade safe forever.
think: **My income** could be hit after 2034, and planning may be automated earlier.
**The warning years** help me save but do not name a reliable next job.
do: Keep **leading site carpentry** while current projects pay.
Review **nearby work** and set aside part of each pay for a transition.
feel: I feel **anxious**, though the warning gives me more room than the 2028 picture.
S3.quote: The extra years help me build savings, but don't tell me what a reliable next job is.
fieldNote: He uses the **warning period** to save while refusing to assume planning work stays human.
He is **less cornered** than in the two-year scenario, though still anxious about income.
He wants a **trusted colleague**'s candid view of the transition.

steps.text: Keep leading carpentry on paid local projects
Set aside part of each pay toward a transition cushion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The interviewer reads the card for AGI by 2036: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is useful time to prepare, but no one should call a trade safe forever. Thinking AI arrives by 2036 and hands-on robots around 2039, so I can judge changes as they appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My income could still be hit when robots do the physical work, even if the longer lead gives me room now. Site planning is thinking work too, so I can't count on moving into an office role as an escape.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll stay in carpentry while local sites hire and review my finances each year. By 2032 I'll ask a trade association about practical retraining options, then decide whether to commit based on what employers actually need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm uneasy about the distant loss of a familiar craft, but not panicked today. Ten years lets me enjoy the work now without pretending the dates are harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which person on your crew would you talk with first, and what would you ask?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Luis what proof he would need before changing our tools, such as a robot working safely around a crew on a real floor. I won't change my livelihood for a polished demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner over dinner that you would leave out of a site conversation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner that we have time to decide together, not a guarantee that my pay stays high. I want us to avoid building plans around a job that might not exist in 2039.

say: **I would say** a decade gives us time to prepare as changes become visible.
**I would not promise** my craft stays protected through 2039.
think: **My physical work** may change around 2039, while planning changes first.
**I cannot count** on an office role as an escape.
do: Stay in **carpentry** while local sites hire and review household finances each year.
Ask the **trade association** about practical retraining by 2032 before deciding whether to commit.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about a distant change, but I am not panicked today.
S4.quote: Site planning is thinking work too, so I can't count on moving into an office role as an escape.
fieldNote: He treats the **ten-year lead** as room to gather evidence, not a guarantee.
His **proposed association inquiry** is exploratory; he has not committed to a course.
He understands **office planning** is exposed before hands-on robots arrive.

steps.text: Stay in carpentry while local sites are hiring
Ask the trade association about retraining by 2032 before committing

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because two years is little time before the planning work changes, with robots following around 2031. Clear information from contractors, a paid transition route and enough notice about projects would help me decide what to do.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I'd ask whether a worker can see and question how the site schedule was made. A wrong sequence costs real hours, and someone on the floor should be able to stop it.

headlineQuote: A wrong sequence costs real hours, and someone on the floor should be able to stop it.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old** senior carpenter who leads a small site crew on mid-rise projects.
His **strong savings** and many local openings give him options, although he shows **resistance** to unfamiliar software.
He separates **thinking tasks**, which change first, from hands-on work, which robots reach about three years later.
He stays calm in a mild scenario and grows **anxious** when near-term robots could cut his income.
He wants **active-site evidence** before changing his work or committing to retraining.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before site planning changes and robots follow around 2031.
He worries his **carpentry income** could fall even with strong skills and a financial cushion.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **clear contractor information** about actual tools and project changes.
A **paid transition route** and notice about projects would help him choose a next step.
